paras: The killing of Henry Small was the shooting of a Black man by a Chesterfield County constable and two other men on a farm near Jarratt, Sussex County, Virginia, on Sunday, July 26, 1903. The men were seeking the attacker of three white women near Centralia five days earlier and shot Small as he ran from them; a coroner's jury called the killing justifiable homicide. Richmond papers had followed the armed manhunt day by day, and the killing was reported as far away as New York.

On the afternoon of July 21 a stranger asked Mrs. R. W. Thompson, a widow of about sixty, for food and water at her home between Bellwood and Centralia, then seized her by the throat and threatened to kill her if she cried out. She fought him off, and he fled when her tenant, Willie Sadler, answered her screams. About an hour later a man said to fit the same description snatched a satchel from Bertha Thurston near Centralia, knocked her down, and drew a pistol on those who followed him.

Armed men searched the woods into the night, "with thoughts of vengeance stirring their breasts," in the Times-Dispatch's words, and the Manchester police heard the fugitive was being "chased by a mob." In the wire account he was tracked to a swamp ringed by "pickets ready to shoot on sight" but doubled on his tracks and got away. The Chester correspondent was told at Centralia that "had the wretch been caught he would have been shot or swung up."

Over the next days several other Black men were held on suspicion and rejected by the women, among them John Balchrop and Ed Pulliam in Richmond and Charles McDonald, seized by citizens near Mineral. Chesterfield constables also set out to drive a "gang" of Black tramps from the woods, and one fired on three men who refused to halt.

According to a Jarratt dispatch, a man who called himself Henry Small had left a freight train at Stony Creek on July 21 and stayed with Alfred Hill, a Black tenant on Luther Creath's farm. Hearing that Small had told Hill's family he had killed a man, Creath compared him with the published description and reported him. On Sunday evening Constable W. H. Moore, with J. H. Batte and C. M. Brown, drove to Hill's house; Small ran out the rear door and ignored orders to halt. Moore fired small shot into his hips and leg, pistol shots followed, and one ball struck him in the back; he died within minutes.

Mrs. Thompson and one of the young women came on the morning train and, according to the Times-Dispatch, identified the body, which bore a swollen lower lip and scratches. A coroner's jury returned a verdict of justifiable homicide; no report of any further inquiry appears in the coverage.

The white Virginia press covered the manhunt under headlines such as "ATTACK MADE ON THREE WHITE WOMEN," called the suspect a "negro fiend" and "brute," and stressed the women's "excellent social standing." When the killing came, the Times-Dispatch announced "THE NEGRO ASSAULTER IS KILLED" and presented the identification, the scars and the coroner's verdict as confirmation.

Accounts of the shooting came from a Jarratt correspondent, a Petersburg wire carried by the New York Sun and the Alexandria Gazette, and a Richmond dispatch to the Washington Evening Star, all giving the posse's version. Most printed as fact Small's reported claim, relayed through Hill's family, that he had killed several men. The Rural Retreat Times headlined its reprint "RAPE FIEND SHOT DOWN," although the charge was attempted assault, and the Virginia Citizen said the man "was thoroughly identified." No Black newspaper account of the case appears in the coverage.

Accounts differ on who fired the fatal shot: the Sun, the Gazette and the Shenandoah Herald named Batte, the Times-Dispatch said "the others" fired, and the Evening Star said Moore alone fired once. The Evening Star also reported that "nobody in the neighborhood can identify the dead man," whereas the Times-Dispatch and Gazette said two of the women identified him after his death.

reader.title: Killing of Henry Small
bases: A Chesterfield constable and two other men, described as a posse, shot and killed a Black man as he fled their attempt to arrest him for the Centralia attacks (A13, A12, A15).

Three men shot Small to stop him escaping arrest for the attacks on the women (A13, A15), but they were led by a constable making an arrest, and a coroner's jury ruled the killing justifiable homicide (A13); no paper reports a mob or crowd at the killing, though earlier reports quote threats to shoot or hang the attacker if caught (A5).

Separate dispatches from Jarratt (A13, A15), Petersburg (A12) and Richmond (A11) agree that a Chesterfield constable's party shot and killed a fleeing Black man in Sussex County as the suspected attacker, though they differ on who fired and on the identification.

accounts.label: Jarratt correspondent (posse's version)
accounts.gist: Moore's shotgun of small shot hit Small in the hips and leg, meant to stop not kill him; pistol shots followed and one ball in the back killed him; the women identified the body and a coroner's jury found the killing justifiable.

accounts.label: Petersburg wire
accounts.gist: Small sprang through a window and ran; Constable Batte fired three shots and he fell mortally wounded; he had said he killed several men.

accounts.label: Richmond dispatch to the Evening Star
accounts.gist: Constable Moore alone, sent by Squire Cheatham, called three times for a halt and fired one ball into the man's left side; nobody nearby could identify the dead man.

framing.detail: The Times-Dispatch headlined 'THE NEGRO ASSAULTER IS KILLED' and reported the coroner's verdict and the scars as confirmation of guilt.
Manhunt coverage called the suspect a 'negro fiend' and 'brute', stressed the 'excellent social standing' of the women, and reported threats of summary vengeance as local feeling.
Out-of-town papers ran short wire versions: 'SHOT THE FLEEING NEGRO' (Sun), 'KILLED BY POSSE' (Gazette), 'CONSTABLE KILLS NEGRO' (Evening Star).
The Rural Retreat Times reprinted the Jarratt dispatch as 'RAPE FIEND SHOT DOWN'.
